title: Se pasiva: Pizarro y el Imperio inca

sections.content: The se-passive reports an event without stating who carried it out — useful when the actor is a vague 'the Spanish' or 'both sides' rather than one named person. These sentences are taken directly from the previous reading.

items.spanish: El 16 de noviembre de 1532, en Cajamarca, se organizó un encuentro entre Atahualpa y los españoles.
items.english: On November 16, 1532, in Cajamarca, a meeting between Atahualpa and the Spanish was arranged.

items.spanish: En cuestión de horas, se masacró a miles de soldados incas.
items.english: Within hours, thousands of Inca soldiers were massacred.

items.spanish: Durante meses se recolectó ese rescate desde templos y palacios de todo el imperio.
items.english: For months, that ransom was collected from temples and palaces across the empire.

items.spanish: En Vilcabamba se mantuvo una resistencia inca continua durante casi cuarenta años más.
items.english: In Vilcabamba, continuous Inca resistance was maintained for almost forty more years.

sections.content: When the thing acted on is a person introduced with the personal a (se masacró A miles de soldados), the verb stays singular even though the "object" is plural — this is what separates a true se-passive (agreeing with its subject: se recolectó ese rescate) from this impersonal-flavored one. Both are extremely common in historical Spanish; don't worry too much about the grammatical label, just recognize the pattern.
